new_statements.rule_in_words: Icen is analysed with four level tones (Top, High, Mid, Low) plus two falling tones (High-to-Low, Top-to-Low); syllable (C1)(C2)(C3)V; the comparative chapter repeats that Icen (with Kutep) has four level tones against Proto-Jukunoid's three. new_statements.identity_note: The snippet carries the section heading '1.1.4 ICEN (Icen)' and the running footer '-72- Icen'; Shimizu's Icen is the Kpan-Icen (Central Jukunoid) language = Etkywan [ich] (Glottolog cites this work as the Glottolog's most extensive description for etky1238; BCCW 1973 equates 'Kentu (Kyato) (= Icen)'). Not Kpan/Kente (treated separately by Shimizu as 'Kpan Knte').

new_statements.rule_in_words: Etkwen (Etkywan/Icen) is a tone language: the suprasegmental system of the syllable/word is lexical tone with three levels, high, mid and low (orthography: acute = H, unmarked = M, grave = L); unlike English it has no strong/weak (stressed/unstressed) syllable distinction, i.e. the author describes no word stress, and tone has no effect on syllable structure (all syllables open, no coda).

new_statements.identity_note: The chapter itself fixes the identity: 'Etkwen, a Jukunoid Benue-Congo language spoken in the south of Taraba State, Nigeria', endnote 1/8: listed as 'Etkywan' in Ethnologue (ISO 639-3 ich) and known as 'Ichen' (hence the Ethnologue code) in Hausa; 'Etkwen = /etkwẽ/'. Same spelling as the 2024 Etkwen New Testament [ich]. Not Kpan [kpk], not Takum Jukun [jbu].

tone_statements.quote: The suprasegmental feature of Etkywan syllables is tone. Rhythmical timing appears to be syllabic, unlike the (alleged) stress timing of English. However, each syllable is marked by tone – register tone, rather than contour tone: either high, mid or low. There are abundant illustrations of tone contrasts particularly in monosyllabic words. (á = high tone; a (unmarked) = mid tone; à = low tone.) <bá>to write, to follow, roof <ba>to thresh, (kind of tree) <bà>to burn, to stick/gum … All vowels take the full tone system.
